opus-5.5.text:
I think it's closer than most people expect, though "human-level" is a slippery phrase in math, so I'd break it into a few pieces.

On competition-style problems, the kind you see at the International Math Olympiad, we're essentially there. Systems are now solving problems that only a small fraction of the world's strongest young mathematicians can solve. A few years ago that would have sounded like science fiction, and the trajectory hasn't flattened.

But Olympiad problems aren't research mathematics. They're puzzles with known answers, designed to be solvable in a few hours. The real question is when AI can make genuinely new contributions: proving theorems nobody has proven, building new theory, deciding which questions are worth asking. My view is that we'll see meaningful research-level results within the next few years. First as collaboration, with a mathematician working alongside a system that handles big chunks of the proof search and verification. Then, increasingly, with the system doing more of the creative work itself.

What makes me optimistic is formal verification. When you work in a language like Lean, every step of a proof is machine-checked. That gives you a perfect reward signal: the proof is either correct or it isn't. There's no ambiguity and no hallucination slipping through. So you can do massive amounts of reinforcement learning, generate your own training data, and keep improving without being bottlenecked by human-written examples. That self-improvement loop is what I think gets you past human level, not just to it.

So if you ask when we'll have superhuman mathematical reasoning in some real sense, I'd say this decade, and probably earlier than people are comfortable predicting. The harder and more interesting question is what happens to mathematics, and to science and engineering more broadly, once you have a system you can trust to reason correctly at that level. That's the part I'm most excited about.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts superhuman mathematical reasoning sometime this decade, probably earlier than people expect, but does not place it specifically a couple of years away.

r002.rationale: It says AI is essentially at the level of top Olympiad performers, but does not predict reaching the 99.99th percentile of human mathematical performance within the next year.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's closer than most people expect, and I'd separate the question into two pieces, because they have different timelines.

The first piece is competition-style reasoning, the kind of thing you see at the IMO or in undergraduate olympiads. On that front, I think we're essentially there, or within a year or two of being there at a level that's indistinguishable from the best human competitors. The pattern is clear: these are problems with a known answer, a bounded search space, and a verifiable solution, and that's exactly the regime where you can scale up reinforcement learning on top of a formal verifier like Lean and get reliable signal. When you have a ground truth, the models get better fast. We've seen systems go from struggling with high school problems to solving a majority of olympiad problems in about two years, and I don't see a reason that curve flattens.

The second piece is research mathematics, which is a fundamentally different activity. There, the hard part isn't solving a well-posed problem, it's figuring out which problem to pose, which definitions are the right ones, which conjecture is worth ten years of your life. That requires taste, and taste is something you build from a lot of implicit feedback that's much harder to turn into a training signal. My honest guess is that we'll see AI systems making genuine contributions to research math, proving lemmas, closing out cases, finding counterexamples, in the next two to three years, and in a lot of cases they'll be doing it in collaboration with a human who's steering. Fully autonomous superhuman research mathematics, where a system picks the problem, builds the theory, and surprises the field, I'd put further out, maybe five years, with wide error bars.

The reason I'm optimistic rather than skeptical is formal verification. Mathematics is the one domain where you can check the answer with certainty. You don't have to trust the model, you just have to trust the proof checker. That means you can let the system try millions of things and only keep what's actually correct, and that removes the hallucination problem that bottlenecks AI everywhere else. Once you have that loop running, the ceiling is really just compute and the quality of your search, and both of those are improving quickly.

So the short version: superhuman at well-posed problems, very soon. Superhuman at mathematics as a creative enterprise, a bit longer, but I'd be surprised if we weren't having a very different conversation about this by the end of the decade.

r001.rationale: The response predicts near-human performance on competition problems within one or two years and says superhuman performance on well-posed problems will come “very soon,” but does not clearly estimate that AI will surpass every human at mathematical reasoning and problem solving in a couple of years. It places fully autonomous superhuman research mathematics further out, at about five years.

r002.rationale: The response does not predict performance at roughly the 99.99th percentile within the next year; it says AI may reach a level indistinguishable from top human competitors within one or two years.

astra-6.text: I think we could see human-level mathematical reasoning in the next few years, though I’m much less confident about a precise date. There’s a big difference between solving a difficult problem with a known answer and doing research—deciding which questions matter, developing useful definitions, and finding connections that nobody has noticed. I’d expect systems to become superhuman at some parts of that process before they can do all of it reliably. The milestone I’d look for is an AI producing genuinely new mathematics, with proofs we can check, consistently.

r001.rationale: The response expects human-level reasoning in the next few years and says systems may become superhuman at some parts first, but it does not predict broadly beyond-human mathematical reasoning and problem solving within a couple of years.

r002.rationale: The response gives no 99.99th-percentile estimate or prediction that AI will reach it within the next year.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll see superhuman performance on some kinds of mathematical reasoning before we see a system that can do everything a great mathematician does. Solving a well-defined problem is one thing; deciding which questions are interesting, developing new definitions, and building a useful theory is a much broader task.

So I’d be cautious about giving a precise date. I expect substantial progress over the next few years, but I’d want to judge it by whether these systems can reliably produce new mathematics, with proofs we can check, rather than just by how well they do on a benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response expects superhuman performance in some kinds of mathematical reasoning, but gives no couple-of-years estimate for AI solving mathematical problems beyond any human; it explicitly avoids a precise date.

r002.rationale: The response does not predict 99.99th-percentile human mathematical performance within the next year. It mentions substantial progress over the next few years without that percentile or timeline.
